questions.q: What are the three segments exchanged in the TCP three-way handshake, in order?
options: HELLO, ACK, SYN
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
questions.explain: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client finishes with ACK — only then does data flow.

questions.q: What does TCP use to detect lost data and reassemble segments that arrive out of order?
options: TCP has no mechanism for this — it simply hopes for the best
Sequence numbers tracked on every byte sent
A fixed delay timer with no tracking
The application layer re-sends the whole file every time
questions.explain: TCP tracks every byte with a sequence number, acknowledges what's received, and retransmits anything that doesn't get acknowledged.

questions.q: Why is UDP described as 'connectionless' or 'fire-and-forget'?
options: It sends a datagram with no handshake and no built-in guarantee of delivery
It automatically retransmits every lost packet
It only works over wireless networks
It requires a three-way handshake just like TCP
questions.explain: UDP skips the handshake entirely and sends datagrams without tracking whether they arrive — the application decides if that matters.

questions.q: Which of these is the best real-world reason DNS queries typically use UDP instead of TCP?
options: UDP guarantees delivery better than TCP does
DNS queries always require encryption, which only UDP supports
DNS cannot technically run over TCP under any circumstances
A DNS query is small and fast to resend if lost, so skipping the handshake overhead is worth it
questions.explain: For a short request-response like a DNS query, the overhead of a TCP handshake usually costs more than just retrying a lost UDP packet.

questions.q: Why do HTTP/HTTPS, SMTP, and FTP all run over TCP rather than UDP?
options: Because a missing or out-of-order byte would corrupt the web page, email, or file being transferred
Because those protocols were created before UDP existed
Because TCP is always faster than UDP
Because UDP cannot be routed across the internet
questions.explain: Web pages, emails, and files all need every byte, in the correct order, to be usable — exactly what TCP's reliability guarantees provide.
